analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the estate tax repeal; it sat in the Finance Committee and died when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the federal taxes owed when large amounts of wealth pass to the next generation: the estate tax, the gift tax, and the tax on transfers that skip a generation. Today those taxes apply mainly to the largest estates; the bill's own text says they raised less than 1 percent of federal revenue. Repealing them would deliver the savings almost entirely to heirs of the wealthiest families, while the lost revenue would have to be made up through other taxes, more borrowing, or cuts to federal programs. The bill never got a hearing or vote in the Senate Finance Committee and died there.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates. The estate tax only applies above a large exemption, so only a small share of estates pays anything; repeal would funnel its entire benefit to families passing down millions of dollars in wealth. A secondary beneficiary would be very large family-owned businesses and farms whose estates face tax bills, though the bill's framing that this is a broad family burden is not what the tax's reach supports.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the entire subtitle of the tax code covering estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes, effective for deaths and gifts after enactment.

Would allow the largest estates to pass wealth to heirs without the 37-55 percent marginal federal tax rates the bill cites, keeping family-owned businesses and farms intact rather than forcing sales to raise cash for the tax bill.
Would eliminate the accountants' and lawyers' work families currently do to plan around the estate tax, and remove the need to buy life insurance just to cover expected estate tax bills.

analysis.who_pays: General federal taxpayers. The bill's own findings concede these taxes bring in roughly $20 billion-plus a year, close to 1 percent of federal revenue; that money funds everything else the government does, so it would have to be replaced through other taxes, more borrowing, or spending cuts. The direct savings would go almost entirely to heirs of multi-million-dollar estates.
analysis.who_pays_short: General taxpayers funding the federal budget

drawbacks.text: The repeal's benefit is concentrated at the very top: because the estate tax applies only above a large exemption, essentially all of the revenue foregone would have gone to heirs of the wealthiest families, not to ordinary households.

Repeal would permanently remove a meaningful revenue stream (under 1 percent of federal receipts, roughly $20 billion a year) that would need to be replaced by other taxes, borrowing, or cuts, per the bill's own findings.

The revenue would no longer be drawn from accumulated wealth, which is taxed lightly at transfer under this repeal; the burden of replacing it would shift toward taxes on work and consumption paid by people who never owe an estate tax.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: it goes overwhelmingly to the heirs of multi-million-dollar estates, while the cost — replacing roughly 1 percent of federal revenue — is spread across everyone who pays federal taxes or relies on federal programs. The bill's family-farm and small-business arguments describe a genuine problem, but a fix aimed only at those estates would cost a fraction of full repeal. As written, this is a large transfer to concentrated wealth with a broad, diffuse cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Senator Jon Kyl introduced the Family Heritage Preservation Act on January 19, 1999, with 19 original cosponsors.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance, which held no markup or vote on it, and it never reached the Senate floor.
26 Republicans had signed on as cosponsors by the end, but the bill received no floor action in the 106th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury kept the estate tax and its revenue, and the heirs of the wealthiest estates did not receive the repeal; the estate planning industry also kept the business the repeal would have removed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury kept estate tax revenue

for.name: Sen. Jon Kyl
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor

for.name: 26 of 55 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill and never scheduled a markup or reported it out, keeping it from the Senate floor

against.name: President Bill Clinton
against.what_they_did: Opposed full estate tax repeal; in 2000 he vetoed the House-passed estate tax repeal bill (H.R. 8), signaling any Senate repeal would have faced the same fate

sides.party_line_note: All 26 cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat signed on; the bill was an all-Republican effort that never advanced.

industries.note: Repeal would spare the largest estates taxes of 37-55 percent on amounts above the exemption, and the bill's own findings put the foregone revenue near 1 percent of federal receipts that other taxpayers would effectively make up.

industries.industry: Family-owned businesses and farms with large estates
industries.note: Owners of taxable businesses and farms would avoid forced asset sales to cover estate tax bills, but only those above the exemption threshold benefit, and that group overlaps heavily with the very wealthy.

industries.industry: Estate planning attorneys, accountants, and trust service providers
industries.note: Repeal would eliminate a large market for estate tax planning, trust setup, and estate-liquidity life insurance; their fees are a real compliance cost on affected families, but the tax also produces revenue for the general budget.
A main use of this insurance is covering expected estate tax bills; repeal would remove much of that demand.
